name: IP Layer Attack Detection — Fragmentation, Spoofing, SMURF, LAND & TTL
description: IP layer attacks abuse fragmentation, source/destination spoofing, and TTL manipulation for IDS evasion, DoS, and firewall bypass. Key attacks: fragmented Nmap scans (IDS/firewall evasion), decoy scanning (fake source IPs), random source DDoS, SMURF (broadcast ICMP amplification), LAND (src=dst), and TTL manipulation to expire before reaching security controls. All detectable via Wireshark IP header field analysis.
source: CDSA Module 08: Intermediate Network Traffic Analysis
notes:
=== IP HEADER FIELDS USED IN ATTACKS ===
  Length          → IP header length
  Total Length    → entire IP packet length (header + data)
  Fragment Offset → reassembly order for fragmented packets
  TTL             → decremented by 1 at each hop; drop when = 0
  Source IP       → can be spoofed — no validation in IPv4
  Destination IP  → can be spoofed — no validation in IPv4

=== FRAGMENTATION ATTACKS ===
Purpose:
  → IPS/IDS Evasion: if controls don't reassemble, they miss payload
  → Firewall Evasion: same — fragmented payload skips inspection
  → Resource Exhaustion: tiny MTU floods reassembly buffers
  → DoS (Ping of Death): packets >65535 bytes crash old OS

Nmap fragmented scan commands (attacker perspective, for detection context):
  nmap <host>        → normal ICMP + TCP SYN scan
  nmap -f 10 <host>  → fragment with 10-byte MTU → many tiny fragments

Wireshark detection:
  ip.flags.mf == 1        → More Fragments flag set (not last fragment)
  ip.frag_offset > 0      → non-first fragment (offset > 0)
  ip.fragment             → all fragmented packets

IOCs:
  → Excessive fragmentation from one host to one target
  → Very small fragment size (MTU 10-20 bytes) = evasion attempt
  → Fragmentation followed by many RST responses = fragmented port scan
  → Pattern: ICMP requests + fragmented TCP SYNs to many ports

Fix Wireshark reassembly:
  Edit → Preferences → Protocols → IPv4 → check 'Reassemble fragmented IPv4 datagrams'

=== DECOY SCANNING ===
Purpose: attacker changes source IP to look like another host (firewall bypass)
Pattern: fragmented ICMP from fake IP, then TCP traffic from real attacker IP
Giveaway: responses (RST for closed ports) go back to real attacker IP

Wireshark detection:
  ip.src == <FAKE_DECOY_IP>     → fragmented ICMP from spoofed src
  ip.src == <REAL_ATTACKER_IP>  → TCP SYN-ACK responses reveal real IP
  → Look for RST packets going TO the real attacker = confirms their IP

IOC: connections started by one IP, continued/responded by different IP

=== RANDOM SOURCE ATTACKS (DoS) ===
Purpose: exhaust connection table or bandwidth on victim
ICMP version:
  → Many random source IPs sending ICMP to victim
  → Victim replies to non-existent hosts (wasted bandwidth)
TCP version:
  → Random source IPs sending TCP SYN to one port
  → Single port targeted, incremental base ports, identical packet lengths

Wireshark IOCs:
  → ip.dst == <VICTIM_IP> with huge variety of different ip.src values
  → All packets same length: identical_length + single_port + random_src = attack
  → Many tcp.flags.syn == 1 to single port from random IPs

=== SMURF ATTACKS ===
Purpose: amplified DDoS — attacker sends ICMP with victim's spoofed src to broadcast
Flow:
  1. Attacker sends ICMP request to subnet broadcast (src=victim IP)
  2. ALL live hosts reply with ICMP to victim's IP
  3. Victim overwhelmed with ICMP replies from entire subnet

Wireshark IOC:
  → Many hosts sending ICMP replies to single victim IP
  → No corresponding ICMP requests from victim (they're spoofed)
  → Fragmentation may appear (attacker adds data to amplify)

=== LAND ATTACKS ===
Purpose: DoS via src=dst spoofing — causes host to talk to itself, exhaust resources
Signature: IP src == IP dst, TCP SYN to same port

Wireshark filter:
  ip.src == ip.dst    → LAND attack signature
  → Also look for: same host sending SYN to itself on same port

Wireshark IOC:
  → Many TCP SYN packets where src IP = dst IP
  → Target port matches active service

=== IP TTL MANIPULATION ===
Purpose: expire packet before it reaches firewall/IDS, not before it reaches target
How: attacker sets low TTL (1, 2, 3) — packet dies at intermediate router, not firewall

Wireshark detection:
  → Open IPv4 header in Packet Details pane
  → Look for unusually low TTL field values (1-5 range)
  ip.ttl < 10        → display filter for low TTL packets

IOC:
  → Port scan traffic with very low TTL values
  → Mix of low-TTL TCP SYN and normal SYN-ACK responses
  → ICMP Time Exceeded messages from routers = TTL expired in transit

Prevention:
  → IDS/IPS/Firewall should reassemble all fragments before inspection
  → Drop packets with TTL below threshold (e.g., < 10 may be suspect)
  → Watch for connections started by one IP taken over by another (decoy scans)
